claim: Ketamine has emerged as one of the most promising therapies for treatment-resistant depression.
source: Over the last two decades, ketamine has emerged as one of the most promising therapies for treatment-resistant depression (TRD) (Krystal et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Krystal et al., 2019

claim: Robust individual differences in response to ketamine have been observed in both healthy controls and patients with TRD.
source: Robust individual differences in response to ketamine have been observed in both healthy controls and patients with TRD (Murrough et al., 2013; Hack et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Murrough et al., 2013 and Hack et al., 2021

claim: A single ketamine infusion results in a response rate of around 65% in patients with TRD.
source: For example, a single ketamine infusion results in a response rate of around 65% in patients with TRD, while individual differences in baseline molecular effects (e.g. NMDA receptor occupancy) and brain function predict the degree to which an individual experiences specific acute ketamine-induced symptoms (Murrough et al., 2013; Stone et al., 2008; Honey et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Murrough et al., 2013; Stone et al., 2008; Honey et al., 2008

claim: At subanesthetic doses, ketamine produces transient changes in behavior, perception, and cognition that are comparable to the positive, negative, and cognitive symptoms seen in patients with psychosis-spectrum illness.
source: At subanesthetic doses, ketamine produces transient changes in behavior, perception, and cognition that are comparable to the positive, negative, and cognitive symptoms seen in patients with psychosis-spectrum illness (Krystal et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citation to Krystal et al., 1994

claim: Ketamine has been shown to increase global brain connectivity (GBC) in the prefrontal cortex (PFC) in healthy controls.
source: For example, ketamine has been shown to increase global brain connectivity (GBC) in the prefrontal cortex (PFC) in healthy controls specifically, and normalize the reduced PFC GBC in patients with major depressive disorder 24 hr post-ketamine (Anticevic et al., 2015; Abdallah et al., 2017; Abdallah et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Anticevic et al., 2015; Abdallah et al., 2017; Abdallah et al., 2018

claim: Ketamine normalizes the reduced PFC GBC in patients with major depressive disorder 24 hr post-ketamine.
source: For example, ketamine has been shown to increase global brain connectivity (GBC) in the prefrontal cortex (PFC) in healthy controls specifically, and normalize the reduced PFC GBC in patients with major depressive disorder 24 hr post-ketamine (Anticevic et al., 2015; Abdallah et al., 2017; Abdallah et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Anticevic et al., 2015; Abdallah et al., 2017; Abdallah et al., 2018

claim: The finding that ketamine increases PFC GBC failed to replicate in patients with depression 48 hr post-ketamine.
source: However, this finding failed to replicate in patients with depression 48 hr post-ketamine (Kraus et al., 2020), suggesting a complex relationship between ketamine's acute and delayed effects.
evidence: Supported by citation to Kraus et al., 2020

claim: Forty participants took part in the ketamine study.
source: Forty participants took part in the study.
evidence: Directly stated in the methods section

claim: The sample size was determined ahead of study initiation based on prior studies which would achieve statistical power of >86% for an estimated medium effect size (Cohen's d of 0.5).
source: The sample size was determined ahead of study initiation based on prior studies Anticevic et al., 2011; Driesen et al., 2008; Johnson et al., 2006; Driesen et al., 2013; Anticevic et al., 2015, which would achieve statistical power of >86% for a estimated medium effect size (Cohen's d of 0.5).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies and power calculation

claim: The study employed a single-blind within-subjects design, with participants blinded to their treatment condition.
source: The study employed a single-blind within-subjects design, with participants blinded to their treatment condition.
evidence: Directly stated in the methods section

claim: Placebo was administered during the first neuroimaging scan session, and ketamine during the second.
source: Placebo was administered during the first neuroimaging scan session, and ketamine (initial bolus 0.23 mg/kg, continuous infusion 0.58 mg/kg/hr) during the second, as residual ketamine effects ruled out counterbalancing of the order.
evidence: Directly stated in the methods section

claim: Participants were able to correctly identify the ketamine infusion 100% of the time.
source: Participants were not informed about the order in which they would receive saline and ketamine, however they were able to correctly identify the ketamine infusion 100% of the time.
evidence: Directly stated in the methods section

claim: The group mean serum ketamine concentration at the end of the resting-state run was 470 nmol/L.
source: Blood was drawn immediately after the resting-state run, and subsequent gas chromatography-mass spectrometry determined that the group mean serum ketamine concentration at the end of this run was 470 nmol/L.
evidence: Directly stated measurement from blood analysis

claim: Ketamine results in five significant neural axes of variation.
source: The PCA performed on the Δ GBC maps revealed ketamine results in five significant bi-directional PCs (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 4) that together capture 42.1% of the total variance.
evidence: Supported by PCA analysis results shown in Figure 2A

claim: The five significant neural PCs together capture 42.1% of the total variance.
source: The PCA performed on the Δ GBC maps revealed ketamine results in five significant bi-directional PCs (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 4) that together capture 42.1% of the total variance.
evidence: Supported by PCA analysis results shown in Figure 2A

claim: PC1 Δ GBC explains 14.1% of all variance.
source: PC1 Δ GBC explains 14.1% of all variance.
evidence: Directly stated in Figure 2D caption

claim: PC2 Δ GBC explains 10.4% of all variance.
source: PC2 Δ GBC explains 10.4% of all variance.
evidence: Directly stated in Figure 2G caption

claim: Ketamine resulted in significantly higher dimensionality compared to LSD and psilocybin.
source: Ketamine resulted in significantly higher dimensionality compared to LSD and psilocybin, while there was no difference between LSD and psilocybin (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by effective dimensionality analysis shown in Figure 2C

claim: There was no difference in dimensionality between LSD and psilocybin.
source: Ketamine resulted in significantly higher dimensionality compared to LSD and psilocybin, while there was no difference between LSD and psilocybin (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by effective dimensionality analysis shown in Figure 2C

claim: PC1 Δ GBC was significantly correlated with the SST cortical gene expression map (r=0.47, p<0.001).
source: For example, PC1 Δ GBC was significantly correlated with both the SST (r=0.47, p<0.001, 100,000 permutations) and PVALB (r=−0.22, p=0.025, 100,000 permutations) cortical gene expression maps, well beyond what is expected by chance alone (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by gene expression correlation analysis shown in Figure 3E

claim: PC1 Δ GBC was significantly correlated with the PVALB cortical gene expression map (r=−0.22, p=0.025).
source: For example, PC1 Δ GBC was significantly correlated with both the SST (r=0.47, p<0.001, 100,000 permutations) and PVALB (r=−0.22, p=0.025, 100,000 permutations) cortical gene expression maps, well beyond what is expected by chance alone (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by gene expression correlation analysis shown in Figure 3E

claim: No significant correlations were found between mean Δ GBC and SST/PVALB cortical gene expression maps.
source: In contrast, no significant correlations were found between mean Δ GBC and SST/PVALB cortical gene expression maps (Figure 3H).
evidence: Supported by gene expression correlation analysis shown in Figure 3H

claim: Ketamine results in two significant bi-directional behavioral axes of variation that together capture 41.4% of all variance.
source: The PCA showed ketamine results in two significant bi-directional axes of behavioral alteration, that together capture 41.4% of all variance (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by behavioral PCA analysis shown in Figure 4C

claim: Behavioral PC1 explains 29% of the variance.
source: Together they capture 41.1% of all symptom variance (inset), with PC1 explaining 29% of the variance and PC2 explaining 12% of the variance.
evidence: Directly stated in Figure 4C caption

claim: Behavioral PC2 explains 12% of the variance.
source: Together they capture 41.1% of all symptom variance (inset), with PC1 explaining 29% of the variance and PC2 explaining 12% of the variance.
evidence: Directly stated in Figure 4C caption

claim: Neuro-behavioral PC1 and PC2 differentiate between association and sensory networks (P<.001).
source: In addition, we found both neuro-behavioral PC1 and PC2 differentiate between association and sensory networks (P<.001), and neuro-behavioral PC1 tracks SST and PVALB gene expression patterns (Figure 5A and B, Figure 5—figure supplement 4E, Figure 5—figure supplement 3A, C, E).
evidence: Supported by neuro-behavioral analysis shown in Figure 5

claim: Neuro-behavioral PC1 tracks SST and PVALB gene expression patterns.
source: In addition, we found both neuro-behavioral PC1 and PC2 differentiate between association and sensory networks (P<.001), and neuro-behavioral PC1 tracks SST and PVALB gene expression patterns (Figure 5A and B, Figure 5—figure supplement 4E, Figure 5—figure supplement 3A, C, E).
evidence: Supported by gene expression correlation analysis shown in Figure 5

claim: Behavioral PC1 scores were highly correlated with neuro-behavioral PC1 scores (r=0.7, p<0.001).
source: The behavioral PC1 scores were highly correlated with the neuro-behavioral PC1 scores (r=0.7, p<0.001), indicating that whether individual variation is captured using behavior or behavior in relation to the neural effect, subjects largely preserve their order (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6C

claim: Neuro-behavioral PC1 showed a significant positive correlation with SST (r=0.29, p=0.009).
source: We found that neuro-behavioral PC1 but not neuro-behavioral PC2 showed a distinct relationship with SST vs. PVALB gene expression maps: neuro-behavioral PC1 showed a significant positive correlation with SST (r=0.29, p=0.009), and non-significant negative correlation with PVALB (r=−0.14, p=0.089; Figure 6E–F).
evidence: Supported by gene expression correlation analysis shown in Figure 6E-F

claim: 35/40 participants exhibit a distinct association with SST and PVALB cortical gene expression maps.
source: We observed that 35/40 participants exhibit a distinct association with SST and PVALB cortical gene expression maps: 23 participants show a positive correlation with SST cortical gene expression maps and a positive negative correlation with PVALB cortical gene expression maps, while 12 participants show the reverse pattern (Figure 6—figure supplements 1–4).
evidence: Supported by individual subject gene expression correlation analysis shown in Figure 6 supplements 1-4

claim: There was a significant positive relationship between each participant's difference in observed SST and PVALB r values and their neuro-behavioral PC1 score (r=0.67, p<0.001).
source: When we formally tested this association by correlating each participant's difference in observed SST and PVALB r values with their neuro-behavioral PC1 score, we found a significant positive relationship (r=0.67, p<0.001; Figure 6H).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6H

claim: The neural geometry of ketamine is multi-dimensional.
source: We show that the neural geometry of ketamine is multi-dimensional, as ketamine results in five significant neural axes of variation, each of which is bi-directional (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by PCA analysis results

claim: The bi-directional nature of the PCs helps explain the contradictory results in the ketamine resting-state literature.
source: The bi-directional nature of the PCs helps explain the contradictory results in the ketamine resting-state literature as the direction of effects is often inconsistent (Höflich et al., 2015; Hack et al., 2021; Grimm et al., 2015; Khalili-Mahani et al., 2015; Kraguljac et al., 2017).
evidence: Inference based on study results and supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Ketamine is a molecule that acts at the same target in every human brain, antagonising the NMDA receptor.
source: Interpreting this finding is of particular interest given that ketamine is a molecule that acts at the same target in every human brain, antagonising the NMDA receptor, which should intuitively result in a single uni-directional principal component (PC).
evidence: Established knowledge about ketamine's mechanism of action

claim: SST interneurons are particularly sensitive to ketamine as a result of their NMDA receptor subunit configuration.
source: SST and PVALB genes were selected a-priori based on: (i) the large body of animal literature directly linking SST and PVALB interneurons to ketamine's acute effects (Gerhard et al., 2020; Ng et al., 2018; Picard et al., 2019); (ii) studies showing SST and PVALB interneurons are particularly sensitive to ketamine as a result of their NMDA receptor subunit configuration (Paoletti et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to Paoletti et al., 2013

claim: PVALB interneurons are particularly sensitive to ketamine as a result of their NMDA receptor subunit configuration.
source: SST and PVALB genes were selected a-priori based on: (i) the large body of animal literature directly linking SST and PVALB interneurons to ketamine's acute effects (Gerhard et al., 2020; Ng et al., 2018; Picard et al., 2019); (ii) studies showing SST and PVALB interneurons are particularly sensitive to ketamine as a result of their NMDA receptor subunit configuration (Paoletti et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to Paoletti et al., 2013

claim: Specific cortical regions express different ratios of SST and PVALB interneurons, with SST showing higher expression levels in association relative to sensory regions, while PVALB shows the reverse pattern.
source: (iii) previous research showing that specific cortical regions express different ratios of SST and PVALB interneurons, with SST showing higher expression levels in association relative to sensory regions, while PVALB shows the reverse pattern (Anderson et al., 2020; Hawrylycz et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citations to Anderson et al., 2020 and Hawrylycz et al., 2012

claim: Patients with depression show reduced SST or PVALB interneurons in areas such as the hippocampus and PFC.
source: (iv) studies demonstrating patients with depression show reduced SST or PVALB interneurons in areas such as the hippocampus and PFC (Nowak et al., 2010; Zadrożna et al., 2011; Czeh et al., 2005; Czéh et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nowak et al., 2010; Zadrożna et al., 2011; Czeh et al., 2005; Czéh et al., 2015

claim: The indirect hypothesis posits that ketamine first inhibits tonic-firing GABAergic interneurons via NMDAR blockade, leading to a burst of glutamate that drives synaptic plasticity.
source: We will focus on the indirect hypothesis, which posits that ketamine first inhibits tonic-firing GABAergic interneurons via NMDAR blockade, leading to a burst of glutamate that drives synaptic plasticity (Gerhard et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gerhard et al., 2020

claim: Ketamine's antidepressant effects are shown to peak 24–72 hr post-infusion.
source: Given ketamine's antidepressant effects are shown to peak 24–72 hr post-infusion, future studies may wish to collect additional follow-up scans (Krystal et al., 2019; Berman et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Krystal et al., 2019 and Berman et al., 2000

claim: Sub-anesthetic doses of ketamine increase heart rate and blood pressure.
source: There is a large body of evidence to suggest that heart rate and blood pressure impact resting-state functional connectivity, and sub-anesthetic doses of ketamine and moderate doses of psilocybin and LSD have all been shown to increase heart rate and blood pressure (Chang et al., 2013; Nikolaou et al., 2016; de la Cruz et al., 2019; Riva-Posse et al., 2018; Bennett et al., 2023; Isbell, 1959).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Moderate doses of psilocybin increase heart rate and blood pressure.
source: There is a large body of evidence to suggest that heart rate and blood pressure impact resting-state functional connectivity, and sub-anesthetic doses of ketamine and moderate doses of psilocybin and LSD have all been shown to increase heart rate and blood pressure (Chang et al., 2013; Nikolaou et al., 2016; de la Cruz et al., 2019; Riva-Posse et al., 2018; Bennett et al., 2023; Isbell, 1959).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Moderate doses of LSD increase heart rate and blood pressure.
source: There is a large body of evidence to suggest that heart rate and blood pressure impact resting-state functional connectivity, and sub-anesthetic doses of ketamine and moderate doses of psilocybin and LSD have all been shown to increase heart rate and blood pressure (Chang et al., 2013; Nikolaou et al., 2016; de la Cruz et al., 2019; Riva-Posse et al., 2018; Bennett et al., 2023; Isbell, 1959).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations
